speechtext: It will have to be with the consent of the House.

maintopic: PAVEMENT IN FRONT OF GOVERNMENT BUILDINGS, WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I informed the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) yesterday that orders had been given for the payment of an amount to the city of Winnipeg for pavements. I find that I was mistaken. I had recommended the matter to council and authority was obtained for the payments, hut they had to be provided for by parliament. My hon. friend will find an amount in the supplementary estimates, and I have no doubt he will he glad to help me in getting these estimates through as quickly as possible.
House again in committee upon resolution to amend the Post Office Act.-Mr. Lemieux.
What is the nature of the examination provided for junior clerks upon entering the railway mail service?

I have not before me the subject matter upon which the candidates are examined, but it is in the nature of the ordinary examination which civil sei'vants must pass. There is a selection of subjects such as grammar, arithmetic, geography and literature. In Quebec the aspirants have the option of using both lan- -guages in the examination. The examinations are not very severe, but still we find it difficult to get the number of men which the service requires. The service is extending so much, with the opening of new routes, especially in the west, where the country is grid-ironed with new railway lines, that we have sometimes to take men who have not passed the examination. But, as I stated before six o'clock, I am making provision for the future in order to be within the law. Not to have to be resourceful in order to evade the law, and at the same time give the public the service required, I have a clause in the Bill which will be based upon this resolution, which will give the Postmaster General authority to employ men who have not yet passed their examination, but who may pass it within a year. Six months after having passed the preliminary examination, clerks, [DOT]not only in the railway mail service but in the service generally, are subject to a promotion examination. They are examined on their special duties. A railway mail clerk would be subject to examination on his route, and on the map of the various railway lines connecting with the line upon which he travels. That is the gist of the examination which they pass.

I am glad to observe that the prospective changes embodied in this resolution are in the right direction, and we are only too pleased to give the minister credit for them. My remarks will apply to the Post Office Act, and what I have to say will be with reference to the service west of the lakes. I will first refer to the letter carriers in the city of Winnipeg, and what I say with reference to the letter carriers, perhaps may apply also to other branches of the service. There, these humble servants of the post office are on meagre salaries. Their work is increasing every year, and under any circumstances, supposing you employ extra hands, still the increase in the business means more work for those who happen to be in the service.
We must remember, too, more especially in the city of Winnipeg and all through the west, rents are very much higher and are increasing every year; living is higher, fuel is more expensive. Many of these are married men; they live up practically to the full amount of their wage; there is very little prospect of promotion, and although we may say that there arq those living in Winnipeg who would take their jobs for the same pay, that is not a fair statement because these men have had a training, and it is only after years of experience they become familiar with their work and with the district they serve. We have another minister who is a little more thoughtful of the people of the west than the Postmaster General, for on page 96 of the estimates we find that the Minister of Inland Revenue has this entry:
Provisional allowance of not more than $125 each to the officers in Manitoba and the provinces west thereof whose salaries do not exceed $1,000 per annum.
The officials of the Inland Revenue Department do not work any harder than those poor fellows who have to trudge the streets of Winnipeg in sometimes bitter weather. If you saw them with the loads they have to carry, you would think it would not be unkind for the Postmaster General to provide them with mules.
Or automobiles.

That would be better still. I call attention to the following statement in the report of the Civil Service Commission at page 28:
Before leaving this branch (the outside service) of their inquiries, your commissioners have to draw attention to the fact that while in the older provinces of the Dominion the struggle for existence is the lot of the average official, yet in the province of Manitoba and British Columbia, and in the Northwest provinces the struggle is intensified. With the long hard winters and the high prices charged for fuel, and also in consequence of
the increased rentals caused by the great boom which lias struck the northwest, your commissioners have had reported to them that the lot of the civil servant in that part of Canada is much more pitiable than that of the civil servant in the older provinces; and whatever .may be the result of these inquiries, your commissioners earnestly commend to the attention of the government the condition of employees in Manitoba and the northwest.
I think that language applies more to the letter carriers than to any other class of persons in that province. The Minister of Agriculture was kind enough to say on the 29th of July, 1909:
I need not point out that the cost of living has immeasurably increased since that time (1857), that the work and responsibilities imposed upon the Civil Service of Canada have greatly increased, and that their relationship to, and standing iu the community, has become so enlarged as to require that they shall have greater consideration in this year of grace 1999 than they had when Canada was a small, inconsiderable and cheap country in 1857.
I call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that there is a great difference in the city of Winnipeg between the conditions in 1909 and in 1911, when these words were uttered. Sir William Mu-lock when Postmaster General had occasion to remark:
The duties of our railway mail clerks are onerous, responsible and hazardous, and with very rare exceptions have been performed with uniform cheerfulness, efficiency and fidelity. I feel fully warranted in saying that Canada has no more deserving and worthy officers than her railway mail clerks.
As applicable to all the civil servants in Winnipeg, not simply the letter carriers, I call attention to a letter signed by Mr. W. L. Ball, manager of the Eastern Townships Bank in Winnipeg, in which he says:
With reference to our conversation as to the cost of living here and in the east, I may say that our hank makes a special western allowance of $300 for each clerk we have in the west.
I support everything that has been proposed in favour of the mail clerks. They deserve every cent of the increase, and I believe the Postmaster General would have been justified in making the increase greater. Not only are their duties arduous, but they are thrust into a post of danger; scarcely a railway wreck but there is some poor mail clerk one of the victims, and it would be pretty hard to properly remunerate that phase of their employment. If the Postmaster General would amend this first resolution and make provision for not less than one hundred and fifty dollars a year extra living expenses for post office employees in Manitoba and the west, he will only be doing what is just and he will have
the support not only of his own party friends, but of the members on this side of the House.

I agree that the cost of living in the west is much higher than in the east, and of course the cost of living, generally speaking, has grown greater year by year fox the last twenty years. The Post Office Department has recognized, just as has the Inland Revenue Department, the principle that a special provisional allowance should be paid to our railway mail clerks, letter carriers, and postal clerks generally in the west. Every year we take a vote in the estimates for that purpose. This provisional allowance is paid to post office employees commencing at Fort William and Port Arthur, and extending throughout Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. Employees in city post offices, including letter carriers, of course, employees in the post office inspectors' office and the office of the Superintendent of Railway Mail Clerks, whose salaries are $800 a year and under, are paid $15 per month or $180 a year provisional allowance. Those officials in the west get $180 per annum provisional allowance over the salaries paid in the east. Then, the provisional allowance to employees whose salaries are over $800 and under $900 is the amount required to make up a total of $980.
The allowance to employees whose salaries range from $900 to $1,200 a year is at the rate of 10 per cent of their salary. The allowance to employees whose salaries range from $1,200 to $1,320 is the difference between the salary and $1,320. The railway mail clerks are paid at the rate of $10 a month when the salary is less than $800 a year, and on salaries ranging from $300 to $1,200 the allowance is 10 per cent on their salary. That is a special provisional allowance paid to our postal clerks, letter carriers, clerks in city post offices, railway mail clerks in the west, and clerks employed in the offices of superintendents and inspectors. So that the increase is quite a substantial one, if we consider what increases have been given since 1896. I fully admit that some years ago, generally speaking, the salaries paid in the post offices, especially to the lower grade men, were a mere pittance. The lower grades in 1896 started at a minimum of $400, and went to a maximum of $800. In 1903, in Sir William Muloclc's time, the minimum was increased to $500, and the maximum to $900, and under the proposed Act this maximum is being expanded to $1,000. Under the Act of 1896 the amount of yearly increase was only $40. This has been raised to $100. There is thus a material increase ever the old conditions. Under the old Act a man would in ten years have a possibility of earning $5,800; under the pro-Mr. BDAGGART (Winnipeg).
posed Act he can earn a total of $8,300, or an increase of $2,500, that is, 43 per cent of liis salary. The second-class clerks in 1896 had a minimum of $900, and went up to $1,200. Under the piuposed Act they will go up to $1,400, which gives them ati increase of 11 per cent, or increased earnings of $1,250 in a period of 10 years. Under the old conditions a first-class clerk started at a minimum of $1,200, and went up by annual increases determined by the Postmaster General until he obtained a maximum of $1,500. Inasmuch as it depended upon the determination of the minister, there was no certainty of the increase being given, and a large number never received it. Under the proposed Act the $1,500 will be increased to $1,800, with a statutory increase of $50 per annum, instead of being subject to the whim or caprice of higher officials or even the will of the minister. This insures regular increases up to the maximum when a man deserves them, and gives an increase of 20 per cent of the maximum, making a difference in ten years of $2,250. The minimum of this class, formerly $1,200, has been raised to $1,400.
What is the difference between the salaries allowed in the west and in the east?

The salaries themselves are not differentiated, but there is in favour of the west a provisional allowance ranging up to $180 or $200 a year. As regards the letter carriers, let me assure my hon. friend from Winnipeg that I have met several of them, and have received many com-, munications from them during the course of this session, and generally speaking they are satisfied with the increase I gave them two sessions ago. At that time they received a very poor salary. Now they receive a minimum of $2.75 a day, plus in the west the $180 a year which I nave mentioned. Besides, let us always bear in mind that much as we may sympathize with the men, and I do sincerely sympathize with them, as my hon. friend does, that they are certain of keeping their situations as long as they wish, they receive two uniforms a year from the department, including their footwear, and, in the large cities where we have tramway services, they get free transportation. This costs the government in Montreal about $8,000 a year, in Ottawa about $8,000, in Toronto about $10,000, in Winnipeg $8,000 or $9,000, and about the same rate in other cities of the west which have tramway services.
Do the railway mail clerks get any uniform or footwear?
No.

I want to make a plea for the railway mail clerk who, under the

new schedule, enters the service at $500 whereas the postman enters at $600 or a little better, and gets his clothes and boots. I think it would be only fair to raise the minimum of the railway mail clerk to $600, so as not to ask them to start at a lower salary than the postmen. I think they are entitled to $600 a year to start with.

My hon. friend must bear in mind that while the letter carriers receive a maximum of only $1,200, the railway mail clerks receive special treatment, getting a maximum of $1,400, plus their mileage. But I am ready to consider the question of clothing the railway mail *clerks. A few days ago I received from a gentleman in Winnipeg-a good Canadian by the way and his views reflect my own- a comment to the effect that the American mail cars are splendidly equipped, beautifully painted, with the talismanic words * United States Mail,' and the Star Spangled Banner and American Eagle blazoned on it, but if you look at a Canadian mail car, provided by our railway companies, to which we pay heavy subsidies, you will simply see the letters 'G.P.O.' inscribed on it, and sometimes nothing at all. You should, he said, urge our railway companies to give us postal cars equal to those supplied by the American companies, I replied that I thought his suggestion was very good, that we should give our mail cars a toilet equal to that enjoyed by the American cars, and equal to that given to the mail^ cars in every other country. I have noticed in France and Germany and England that the mail cars there are conspicuous^ by their external decorations. But coming to the employees inside, I admit that there is something in the suggestion of the hon. member for Toronto "(Mr. Russell) that perhaps our railway mail clerks should have a uniform. As regards the scale of salary, however, that is a question of policy for the government. It is not merely my own volition that I have to follow in the increases I submit to the committee, but the matter is one which pertains to the government as a whole, and we must take into consideration not only the opinion expressed by my hon. friend, but also what the public thinks about it, and what the administration of public affairs warrants. Let us not forget that besides the increases in salaries which we have given since a few years, we have also given to the public the benefit of many material decreases in postal rates. I shall not weary the House by recounting these decreases, but I think we have given the public very substantial decreases in postal rates, and we intend to follow the same progressive policy in the future. If the House will 'leave to my tender care the employees of the Post Office Department, the clerks will not regret it. They have been satisfied in the past with what in-282
creases I have obtained from parliament for them, and I think they will be in the future. Of course many would like a little more. That is only human nature. But we must stop at some point, and I think that on the whole the policy I have explained is in the right direction in so far as the resolutions I have submitted to the House are framed according to the Civil Service Act, and with the view of bringing the clerks in the large city post oflices under the Act in the near future.

I heartily concur in the legislation which the hon. the Postmaster General has submitted, but as regards the salaries of the officers in western Canada especially, I desire to point out that there is a greater difference between the conditions at Winnipeg and those in eastern cities than has been met by this legislation. A clerk in any occupation in the city of Winnipeg gets more salary today than he would in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto, for doing the same work, and the extra allowance provided for letter carriers in Winnipeg does not make up the difference. The Winnipeg letter carriers are among the hardest worked officials of the government. Winnipeg is a very big city, the routes are long, and the mails to be carried are very heavy.
And many foreign settlements.

They are a very efficient class of men and worthy of the best treatment. I believe that the Postmaster General is trying to do what is right. I believe he is trying to make legislation which will apply to all parts of the Dominion as fairly as possible, but there is a great difference between the wages in western Canada and in eastern Canada. What might be a fair salary in Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal, would not be considered at all adequate in Winnipeg. If you pay your letter carriers in Winnipeg only the same salary as you do in Ottawa or Montreal, I do not think you are treating them fairly and I do not think that the extra allowance will make up the difference, 10 per cent, I understand, is the basis of your extra allowance. I hold that the increased cost of living is much greater 'than ten per cent in the west over the cost in the east. These letter carriers have to be very intelligent, and the men who are doing that work in Winnipeg should command a higher salary than they are now doing. Of course, as the minister has pointed out, their position is permanent, but I do not think they come under the Civil Service Act.
Under the Post Office Act.
Are they entitled to superannuation ?
The older men who were appointed before the Superannuation Act was abolished are, but not the others.
Then there is no provision for these men after they have served as letter carriers for 15 or 20 years.
No.

In view of that fact the government should at least give these men salaries equal to any they could command in the cities where they are employed, I fear this has not been done in Winnipeg. The minister knows well the increased cost of living in the west in comparison with the east, and must realize that the extra allowance to a man getting a salary less than $800 is not going to make up the difference between the salary he is getting and that which he would command in any other occupation in the city of Winnipeg. I would urge strongly that either the extra allowance or salaries be increased. Just a word about the mail clerks. I want to emphasize*what the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) and other gentlemen have said about the mail clerk service.
There are no men in the employ of the government who are entitled to greater consideration than the men who take charge of the mails on railway trains. They endanger their lives every time they enter their cars and in addition it is a most unhealthy occupation. A mail clerk on the train impairs his health more than any other government official. I have been told by porters on Pullman cars that the average usefulness of a porter is less than 18 years, I presume owing to the motion of the car and the consequent injury to his health. If that is so, the mail clerk occupies just as unhealthy a position as the porter, and anything the Postmaster General has done for the mail clerks will be appreciated by the people of Canada. I believe he could go even further than he has done, and would still receive the support of every man who knows anything about the services rendered by these mail clerks. I would urge the minister to take the western part of Canada into consideration. He realizes .that there is a great difference between the men performing these services in western Canada and all other government officials there; that they are entitled to greater pay proportionately than they receive in eastern Canada on account of the extra cost of living, and the extra work they have to do. In Winnipeg the post office officials are worked very hard, the city is growung very rapidly, and it sometimes taxes the ingenuity of the service to handle the mail matter that goes into that city. I would urge upon the minister to increase either the salaries or extra allowances of letter carriers in Winnipeg.
Mr. BRADBURY,

I wish to endorse what has been said. The railway mail clerks of the east should also come in for some consideration if the minister contemplates an increase in pay to the mail clerks in the west. The railway mail clerk has very arduous duties, his quarters are very cramped and poorly ventilated, and all the conditions that he has to meet with tend to make his life rather a life of hardship. With all this he has a great deal of responsibility, having complete, and absolute control over all the matter in the mail car, registered mail and all other things of the kind. Besides that he literally takes his life in his hands every time he goes on the train. The railway mail clerks should receive the first consideration, because their duties are very hard, and even the post office clerks, I think, receive a very small salary to start on, $500. $400 twenty years ago was worth more than $500 or $600 today, and as the country progresses the government should increase the remuneration of their employees if they wish to keep up the standard of their service. The mail clerks and the post office employees have responsible duties which they perform generally very well. There are very few complaints against the post office in this country. Small payment means poor service in everything. The increase which has been made from $400 to $500 seems a very small one, and the government would find many sympathizers if they could see their way clear to raise the salaries of these people who are doing the hard work in the department. I am well aware that there are many soft snaps in the department where officials are paid relatively much higher salaries. To the railway mail clerks and post office clerks, who actually do hard work, more than $500 should be paid.

I would ask the Postmaster General to try and place this salary limit a little higher. I am perfectly satisfied with the increase of $200, and I think the men will all be satisfied. It is a long time since the old scale was fixed and probably it will be a long time before this one will be changed. I think the Postmaster General should make the increase of $200 general all along the line, and should give the clerk entering the service $600 where he had $400 before, just as he has raised the $1,200 limit to $1,400. That, I think, would satisfy all concerned. I find that an increase of $50 a year amounted' 16 cents a day, or 4 per cent of a man's salary of $1,200. I consider that that increase is too small considering the increased cost of living. The poorer class of labouring men in Toronto are to-day getting 50 per cent to 75 per cent more than they got 10 or 15 years ago. This increase of 4 per cent seems to be hardly anything at

all. A man in the service who is within two or three years of the top of his class will go on getting the regular increase to which he was entitled, and then he will have to work along three or four years more to get to the top of the new class, so he would have to be of a good age before he would get to the maximum of the new class. I think what I contended for this afternoon is nothing more than fair, that the increase should be general all along the line. Where a man is near the top of his class he should hold the same position in the new class with that increase of $200. I want to ask the Postmaster General if he can hold out any hope of increasing this scale?

While there is life there is hope. I have given a resume of the policy of the government for the present year. I think the postal clerks, the mail carriers and the railway mail clerks have no fault to find with the increases I have given. Of course, as I said a moment ago, it is human nature to ask for more, but there must be a stopping point. We must advance progressively towards better salaries, we cannot expect to reach high water mark at once. All I can say is that I have taken into consideration the remarks made by the hon. gentleman, and in the future I shall certainly do my best to meet each case as it arises. Speaking about this provisional allowance for the west, although the cost of living is higher in the west, yet we must not forget that an additional sum of $15 a month, besides the salary paid to the clerk, is quite a bonus to the western clerks. Certainly they should be satisfied with that. A clerk receives $800 a year, and if he resides at Port Arthur, or Fort William, or Winnipeg, or any other point west of Lake Superior, he receives an additional sum of $180 a year. Certainly they cannot ask the Post Office Department to do more. The high cost of living is recognized, and we pay accordingly. My hon. friend says that $500 to begin with is a very small salary. Now I make an appeal to his common sense and his knowledge of business. Go to the city of Toronto, or the city of Ottawa, and you will find young men 18 or 20 years of age, unmarried, fresh from school or college, having received a fairly good education, though perhaps not a - high education, and if they knock at the door of the Bank of Montreal here in Ot-tavpa, or the Bank of Ottawa, or of any insurance company, what salary will they receive? Look at a young man in the Bink of Montreal as a clerk, with a nice dress, a high collar and nice cuffs, receiving the public with a smile behind the wicket, receiving dollars, and notes, an 1 heaps of money from the public-what salary does he receive? Sometimes only $403 I have known cases in the best banks in the coun-' 282*
try where young clerks receive only $350. They consider the position' very desirable, because they learn the business, and they come in contact with the business public. How are increases given in those banks? Are they given by the hundred, or by the two hundred? According to my knowledge they receive less than that. I know many clerks in the banks, married men, who would be glad to receive after ten or fifteen years a salary of $1,500. Now take the railway mail clerk. Of course he knows what risks he has to run on the railway trains, but he accepts those risks joyfully. We generally have more applications for the position than we can fill. After a few years, if they behave well, they receive increases in salary, and are afforded chances of promotion, and pass automatically from one class to another. The best men in the service to-day, the men who are the rock bottom of the Post Office Department, are men who came in at $500 or $400 a year. Take the case of George Ross, general post office superintendent for the whole Dominion. There is a man with twelve children, a Scotchman, with a French Canadian family.
No Irish?

No Irish in him except the wit, he is a very witty man. He worked his way up in the department until he became practically indispensable in the service. There is nothing to good for George Ross, in my estimation, because he knows the business from A to Z. He started at the beginning. Take the case of Mr. Gabou-ry, assistant postmaster at Montreal. There is a young man with a classical education, and who, for family reasons, accepted at first a very modest employment in the Montreal post office. He started at the beginning, and worked his way up until he became second only to Mr. Ross. Take the case of Mr. Green, the inspector in Quebec; take the case of the postmaster in Winnipeg. The best men in the west have all come from the east, because we were creating new districts in the west. They are all men who began at the very beginning, and worked their way up intelligently, courageously, until to-day they are receiving good salaries. But the clerk who has no ambition, who has no grit in him, will remain in his class, receiving his $50 increase, and will pester the minister, pester the members, both Grit and Tory, will pester the officials of the department, to get him a higher salary. Is not that a true picture of the existing evils in the service? The man who is willing to work, and fight his own way, to fight the battle of life bravely, that man will inevitably pass into the higher grades, and is bound to succeed. That is my experience.

I am afraid I have been labouring under a delusion. I have been fighting for a class of men that the Postmaster General tells us does not exist. I was not aware until now that he was getting bank clerks to work in the railway mail service. I am surprised to hear it. There is a reason why banks employ such cheap labour. The .young fellows they employ, as a rule, come from rich families whose parents can find nothing else for them to do, and who are glad to get them into some bank where they are satisfied to work for almost nothing.

Take a young man out of a high school in Ontario, who has received a very good education, and if there is no favouritism, no nepotism exercised in his favour, he will go to a bank, or an insurance company, and will be glad to take a position. They are not from rich .families, far from it.
They are serving an apprenticeship.

I thought I was fighting for men who had reached the age of 21 or more, who had some responsibility in life, and who probably had families to provide for, or widowed mothers, or something like that. I did not know that the department could secure railway mail clerks enough at from $300 to $500 a year. If they take them at 18 years of age and can get all they need, 1 am afraid there will not be much room for me to argue on their behalf. But, I was under the impression that a man had to be of the age of 21 years to enter the service, that he had to pass an examination, and I thought that the department would probably require a man with some responsibility about him and with some sort of matured mind to take charge of a railway mail car. I thought that the responsibility of the position called for the engagement of men instead of boys. That is the reason I look upon the salary of $500 as being far too small. I was figuring that a responsible, intelligent man should really start at $600 and work his way up. I would ask the Postmaster General if he could find it in his heart now to amend his Bill so as to make the yearly increase, if it has to be a yearly increase, $100 instead of $50 all along the line, make it $100 up to $800, or, if he can do so, amend the Bill so as to make it $100 a year increase until they get to the top of their class, and apply it to all the men in the service who are receiving more than $800 a year up to $1,400. I think that is fair. If we cannot get the whole loaf we will have to be satisfied with a half, and I suppose we will have to be satisfied with anything we can get, but I would ask the Postmaster General if he could not see his way clear to amend the Bill so as to provide that railway mail clerks shall get $100 a Mr. LEMIEUX.
year increase until they get to the top of their class, and postal clerks as well. That $100 yearly increase should be made general. When the minister considers that $50 is only 16 cents a day I think he will realize that twice 16 cents is not very much of an increase to these men who have been waiting three years for it. There is no question that if the inside service received their increase on account of the high cost of living, these other men have had to put un with the high cost of living as well. They were then entitled to an increase, and if they had received it at that time they would now have very nearly reached the top of their class. I ask the Postmaster General in all seriousness if he will not promise to make that amendment to the Act. I think I am asking only for what is fair. I am not here to boost salaries, I have the interests of the country as much at heart as anybody else, and I think I am asking for only what is iust and fair. Will you promise it, Mr. Postmaster General, if you please?
I do not like to make promises that cannot be implemented.
If you give your word I guarantee it will go through.

I know that my hon. friend is in earnest in his request, but the resolutions that are submitted to the House represent the policy of the government. As I have explained to the committee, these Bills will follow the lines of the Civil Service Act. We cannot change these increases. They will follow the increases in salaries in the corresponding classes of the inside service.
How about the $150 flat increase to the Civil Service?

But these officers are not yet in the Civil Service. I said this afternoon that when the outside service, as is contemplated, is brought under the Civil Service Act, I can promise my hon. friend, if not a flat increase, at least a fair consideration of a flat increase, but I cannot say more than that.

While the poor fellows who are in the outside service have the benefit of a minister such as we have at the head of the postal department, I think we should take advantage of the fact and increase the scale to what is right, because I am afraid that if they come under the Civil Service Act they will get into the hands of another minister, and they will have a poor chance for advancement. Let us try and fix this up before they come under the tender mercies of this other minister. I think that would be a fair thing to do.
I have travelled with them day in and day out.

If there is any truth in the statement that the life of a Pullman conductor is only ten or twelve years, I do not see how it would be possible for a railway mail clerk to get up to the maximum of his class if that time represents his working years, and I think that he should get the small increase that has been asked for on his behalf. I also think that the car should be improved. You might have that beautiful flag that I like so well painted upon the side of the car. It would be merely an act of justice to give more salary to the railway mail clerks. The railway mail clerks are a good class of men, and I am surprised at the statement that it is difficult to get good ones. I know that the railway mail clerks running in and out of London are first-class men, and I do not know where you can get better ones. The employees in the post office are not any better although those who occupy those positions are of a superior class. It should not be difficult to get good men to fill these places. I know that when the higher positions are to be filled it is not difficult to get men. They do not take men who have been in the post office service when they desire to fill these higher positions. I hope the Postmaster General will see his way clear to give these men the consideration to which they are entitled.

It is not very often that I address this House on the question of the Civil Service; in fact, I have never made any remark upon the subject, but once in my life. In my opinion there is no class of men who are paid so well as civil servants both in the inside and outside services. They are not giving anything like the service which is being given to the banks, insurance companies and commercial establishments, and I believe I am safe in saying that on the average they are receiving fifty per cent more salary than like ability and service would command in any other walk in life in Canada. Never a month goes by in this House that I do not hear members advocating an increase of salary for somebody. Why, we are granting salaries around the city of Ottawa that I am heartily glad my constituents do not know anything about. I do not send the
blue-book containing the civil list home, because I do not want them to know anything about it. I perhaps feel a little bit sore about this question. It is some time since my hon. friends have recommended people for these positions, but when the time comes, if it ever does come in their lifetime, they will find that they will not have any difficulty in getting enough people to fill these positions at the salaries provided. The only difficulty now is to weed out from the great number of applicants the proper parties. I do not know that any minister will say that he has ever found any difficulty in finding men willing to take these positions. My experience is that they will apply for these positions, and you would think that they would be happy for the rest of their lives, but it won't be three months before they are back looking for an increase of salary. I believe we are responsible for that through giving in to them too much; there seems to be no man with stamina enough to get up and say: You are overpaid now. Railway mail clerks have been receiving perhaps less for their labour than do other classes of civil servants, but I think the minister has very well met the deficiency in the resolution before t-hei House. While my hon. friend from Toronto no doubt speaks from the very best motives possible, I think he is a little unreasonable. You will find there will be no railway mail clerk resigning because he did not get a greater increase. I repeat that the civil servants of this country are paid fifty per cent more than any other class of labour of equal ability and equal service. I think we are granting clerks as much as they are entitled to. and as much as the taxpayers of Canada can afford.

It was refreshing to hear the candid remark of the Postmaster General to the effect that if a man in the service, particularly the railway mail service, were to expect advancement he must have some grit in him. However, it was not any more refreshing than to hear the member ot Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell), advocate anything in this House in the direction of lessened expenditure. That feature of the discussion this afternoon is one of the most remarkable things that has ever occurred in this House since confederation. Now, I believe there is a very great difference between a man on a railway train acting as mail clerk, and a man in the inside service or a bank clerk. We must in all fairness consider the responsibility of the position of the mail clerk, the dangers attendant on it, the long hours of labour, and the fact that for a good part of the time he is away from his family, while the inside civil servant or the bank clerk

is enjoying the comforts of home. It seems to me that the minimum salary at which railway mail clerks commence is small. I would ask the Postmaster General if the retiring age is 65 years?

There are railway mail clerks who are in good health, and who are past that age limit: Under the old superannuation system, they can be superannuated when they reach the age of sixty or sixty-five, but that only applies to a few cases now. If they are in good health, they are not forced to resign.

A man who has been a mail clerk for twenty years, and reaches the age of sixty-five years will not in my opinion, be in very good health. He may have been robust when he entered the service, but he will have his health pretty well shaken up by the time he reaches that age. Now, what the Post Office Department should do is, when railway mail clerks attain a certain age, put them in the inside service and let younger men get out on the road. If a man has efficiently served as railway mail clerk until he reaches the age of fifty-five, he should be given a position in the inside service where he would be able to experience the comforts of home life.

That is just what
happens in the service to-day.
Yes, if a man has pull enough to get there.

It is not a question of pull. I would be ashamed of myself if I took stock only in the pull that employees may have. The only reproach I receive is from men with pull who are disappointed in not getting what they wish. Not long ago Mr. Talbot, the Railway Mail Superintendent, at Quebec, who has been in the service for years, required assistance in his office, and I took a railway mail clerk, who had seen twenty yeaTS service, and put him in the position of Assistant Post Office Superintendant. He lost his mileage by accepting the position, and I had an order in council passed granting him the mileage he would have been entitled to had he kept his run. That man is perfectly satisfied, but other railway mail clerks, who are only thinking of the pull they could use with the minister, were very mad because I selected a gentleman who had been appointed under the old government. You cannot bluff the public that way; a man who has rendered faithful service is generally, and in my department always, first choice. I look to the men who have not simply fulfilled their duties with more or less efficiency, but men who have shown intelligence and love of their work, and I promote them, as in the case mentioned, Mr. EDWARDS.
without caring for what pull other men may have.

My reason for mentioning ' pull ' is because of the evidence I have in my own very county where political pull seems to be brought into play even in such a little matter as appointing a postmaster who gets $35 a year. About a week ago I called the attention of the Postmaster General to this case in my own county; the father was appointed postmaster, and for nine years his son had discharged the duties faithfully and satisfactorily, and when I asked that the son be appointed postmaster I am told that I should get a letter from the president of the Grit association of the county of Frontenae, and if I did so it would be done. Knowing the president of the Grit association, I spoke to him personally about the matter, and his reply was that it would probably take two or three weeks, as he had written to that part of the county to get the opinion of half a dozen or more people as to whether he should recommend the appointment of this man who, for nine years, had given satisfactory service, or whether he should recommend some one else.
That is the reason why it occurred to me that possibly a pull was necessary to a man to get promoted. Not only do the men who do service as mail clerks on the train have an unpleasant life, being deprived of many of the pleasures which other people have, but a comparatively small percentage of them live to say 55 years of age. It seems to me, speaking as a medical man, that their occupation must necessarily be a very unhealthy one, not only because of their cramped quarters in the mail car, but because of the constant shaking of the train, and every consideration should be given to these men. If I understand this resolution aright, the maximum salary is $1,400. This is as high as a man can expect to reach, no matter what his ability is. I do not see that a man has a great chance of making his way in the world, or is given very much encouragement at this rate. He starts at $500. and is allowed an annual increase of $100 until his salary reaches $800; that will take three years, and then he has $50 a year increase until it reaches $1,400. He will be 15 years in the service before he reaches the splendid salary of $1,400 a year, and there he stops. That is as high as he can go as far as that provision is concerned.
Plus his mileage.

That makes a difference, but I think the minimum salary [ should be at least $600. I think the length

of time for the annual increase of $100 should be lengthened from three years -to five years at least.

I crave the indulgence of the committee in order that I may bring to the attention of the minister a subject to which I do not observe any reference in these resolutions. I understand that a deputation of postmasters from the towns and villages and country post offices waited on the minister last winter and urged upon him certain privileges and reforms, as well as something better in the way of remuneration. I want to emphasize my thorough accord with the request of these men. The country is indebted to the country postmaster to a very great extent, much more than to the men who are in the service in the cities. Not that I wish to make any comparisons, because comparisons are always odious; but the postmasters in the country, and in the towns and villages give services to the public for which they get no remuneration whatever from the public except their good-will, and in these days of high prices and high cost of living good-will will not go very far towards paying for a square meal or a barrel of flour. I want to urge on the Postmaster General the necessity of being more liberal in respect of the country end of his department, which I think is the largest end. I am satisfied that it is the end that gives him the most faithful service. When he is in bed sleeping the sleep of the just, the country postmaster is very often up waiting for the mail bag, and he really gets nothing for doing so. In view of the fact that the service has flourished as well as it has under the care of the present Postmaster General,.I think that a little of the surplus in his department might go to ameliorate the condition of these men. I do not wish to detain the committee at any length on the subject, but I would like to hear the views of the Postmaster General while we are discussing this resolution, so that they may be a matter of record.

I told them that any ai the postmasters who cared to see the annual report of the department might apply to the member or the minister, and he would get it. We send them the postal guide and in that they can get the information they require, but it would cost an enormous amount to distribute among 15,000 postmasters that bulky report-and for what reason? Many of them would not read it. That report contains details of expenditure which are of use to members of the House or specialists, but are not required by postmasters. However if any postmaster should require the annual report, I would be only too pleased to give it to him at his request.
My hon. friend states quite truly that the Post Office Department depends largely on the intelligence, integrity and fidelity of the rural postmasters for the service of His Majesty's mails, and I quite agree with him that in the near future we must yield to the reasonable request which they made when they came here in January last.

In my constituency there is a very large mileage, and a number of these letter carriers employed, and I cordially endorse all that has been said regarding an increase of salary to them. I was somewhat surprised at the attitude taken and the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). To say that there are other men who would be glad to take the places of these men is not an answer to the claim that they should have a fair salary. There are always men ready to take another man's place, and that is a very unfair argument for refusing to pay a fair remuneration to the holders of the office. There is scarcely any position in life, no matter how inadequate may be the salary attached to it, which you will not find outsiders ready to take. While possibly down in his portion of the country these men were receiving fair wages foT the labour they did, in our western country the cost of living is considerably higher, and that cost of living has gone up all over the country, so that what might have been a fair remuneration a number of years ago would not be at all fair to-day. I heartily endorse the argument of my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) with regard to our western country. The rapid development of that country has brought about a condition of affairs in which men are in some cases making very much more money than they could down east. It is apt to cause an unrest, an uneasiness among these men who fee1!, looking at their neighbours making larger sums of money, that their salaries look small. Therefore, it would probably tend to a better service along the lines suggested by the Postmaster General himself,- there would be an esprit de corps, men would feel that they were being recog-Mr. LEMIEUX.
nized and their good work appreciated and they would take a deeper interest in their *vork, and you would get a better class of service. I a.m glad that is the stand that is being taken, and I hope it will guide the Postmaster General in dealing with this question.

I have a suggestion to make and I make it with a pretty strong hope that it will be adopted, because I have always found the Postmaster General willing to consider any reasonable proposition, and to do anything within the bounds of reason for the benefit of the public or to remedy a wrong. I would suggest that the increase of $100 a year proposed to be given from $500 to $800, should continue until the $1,400 is reached. That would take nine years. It would seem to me a man should reach the maximum of $1,400 in nine years. I rather find myself disagreeing with some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House because I pretty fully agree with the propositions made by the Postmaster General in these resolutions. I think he is making a very fair allowance for the services rendered.

The railway mail clerks and others will be satisfied to receive the increase proposed, and as occasion may arise, as it will in the future, I will certainly consider the requests made this evening by hon. members.
Is this provision for the increases of $100 a year to $800 and $50 after that, in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act?
Yes.

I am glad the Postmaster General proposes to increase the salaries of the rural postmasters, but I do not think he has gone far enough, I do not know how many there are getting these very small salaries. I shall not ask anything like what the minimum salary shouid be, as it would be such a contrast, but just fancy a postmaster in a rural part of the country, in a little village where he is at the beck and call of every citizen in the neighbourhood, perhaps from six o'clock in the morning until nine o'clock at night for 312 days, getting $100. It seems a trifling sum for that service. They have been receiving only $35.

My hon. friend must not forget that they receive at the same time a commission on the stamps sold, and of course many of these offices where the minimum is $35, do not earn the salary. For instance, the other day I opened an office at Bark Lake, in Arganteuil, for summer visitors. We had to advertise for the courier service and pay the courier, the office is open for four months and the postmaster receives $35 in addition to the

commission on the stamps he sells. Where a postmaster is obliged to be on his feet for ten or twelve hours a day he receives much more than $35, and of course he has the commission on the stamps, and at such an office he receives mails at night and in the day time, for which there is an extra allowance, so they are not so badly treated. We all admit the salaries at some of the little country offices are very small, because these offices must be kept open at any cost, in order to give the public newspapers and letters. I quite agree that the fact of keeping .an office open to the public, whether the postmaster is kept busy or not, should imply the payment of a decent salary, and 1 contemplate in the near future to give the rural postmasters another lift.
Will the Postmaster General give me an idea of the additional income from the sale of stamps and from other sources, where the salary is only $35?

He receives 40 per cent on the sale of stamps, and besides, receives a fuel allowance and a light allowance. Many of those small country offices afford "$500, $600 to $700 a year; it depends upon the business of the locality. But there are some offices where the business transacted does not amount yearly to $15, or even $10. But we must have an office there. Where there is a small settlement we must give them a mail service, and we pay the postmaster at least $35, plus whatever commission there is on the sale of stamps.
. Mr. CROTHERS. The minister says we must have an office, and we must have a postmaster. That postmaster becomes a public servant, and he ought to be fairly remunerated for the service he renders. Now the postmaster, at these little country offices, is at the beck and call of every one from seven in the morning until nine at night. He sells $25 worth of stamps a year, which would give him $5 additional.
And about $15 extra as an allowance for fuel and light.

That would be $60 foT 312 days. I am not speaking of these little offices that are opened for the convenience of tourists in the summer time But I am not making an unreasonable request of the Postmaster General that, instead of making the minimum $50, he make it $60. That will only give a trifle of over $1 a week extra for six days' service. I think that is reasonable.

I have to leave for home in a few minutes, and before I go I would like to make one more appeal to the Postmaster General. I know7 he would like to
see me going home happy, and if he will promise to make that increase $100 a year instead of $50, and raise the minimum from $800 to $1,400, I would go home as happy as could be, and I know that there are hundreds of mail clerks throughout the country who would also be made happy. I want to say a word with reference to something that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) said a little while ago. It is probable he has seen some of the civil servants around Ottawa when he says they do not earn their money. But I know railway mail clerks who have to leave their homes at six o'clock in the morning and hurry off to get their trains, and who don't get back home again until ten at night. I think when a man puts in that number of hours he earns his pay pretty well.
Does the hon. gentleman know of railway mail clerk's in Toronto who are performing a service like this every day in the w7eek? Or is it only one day, and then he lays off for a few days?
Would the hon. member expect any man to perform that service every day in the week?

I do not expect it. But my hon. friend is putting that forward as an argument, and one would infer .from his argument that that was the case. I know that is not the case, because no man could stand it.

If you divide the number of hours that man puts in throughout the week, he puts in over eight hours a day every day in the week. You can't expect him to go out every day and work 16 or 18 hours in the day. One word more. Won't the Postmaster General please, please grant that little request, and make that increase $100 instead of $50? Then I will sleep happy.

I am very sorry, but if I were to grant his request which he makes so vehemently, though it might give him a happy sleep, it would give me a nightmare.
' Before framing this Bill, I consulted even some of the railway mail clerk's. I had a visit the other day from one of the oldest of the mail clerks in the service, who declared himself perfectly satisfied with the provisions in the Bill. Why, Sir, some of the railway mail clerks, when they reach the maximum will be receiving the indemnity of a member of the House of Commons, with the mileage. Do not you think, Mr. Chairman, that it is going a little bevond the mark to insist that we should give them so much? I think they are well treated. I think to-morrow the railway mail clerks and the postal clerks will be satisfied. The work performed by a railway mail clerk, in my judgment, does not

compare with that of the letter carriers, yet the letter carriers receive only $2.75 a Jay.
They have regular hours, and the mail clerk does not.

The letter carrier has to keep walking up and down the streets, he has sometimes to go up two flights of stairs, and wait at the door, in good weather or bad weather. I think their case is a stronger case than that of the mail clerk. I do not minimise the services rendered by the railway mail clerks, but when we give .them an increase of $200 over tfce maximum they have already had, they should be satisfied, and I think as a matter of fact they are satisfied.

The Postmaster General told us to leave this matter to his tender mercies. In so far as the Postmaster General personally is concerned, and as long as we have to have the government opposite I am quite willing that he should hold that position. Like many other hon. members on this side of the House I was struck with the statement of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). I have often thought I would like to see the hon. member for Carleton standing on a good solid foundation, and making a good solid argument on some honest, fair case; I believe he could do himself justice. I. have heard him on a good many occasions when he has not had that advantage and he has always been able to put up a fair argument-I would like to have heard him a little over a year ago when we were passing $350,000 to distribute amongst the civil servants of Ottawa. I wonder where the hon. gentleman was on that occasion, and why he did not stand up and protest against it.
I am sure he would have given us some information on an occasion of that kind, that he would have done himself justice and that he would have had a good many admirers in this House. I have nothing to say against a man getting all he can get in so far as salary is concerned, but I must express my regret that in place of the resolution we have before us to-night we have not had presented to us a proposition to place the outside service, and particularly the railway mail clerks, under the Civil Service Act. It would be a great advantage not only to the Postmaster General himself but to the old country, and to those who are engaged in that service. I would also like to say a word in connection with the argument that has been made here tonight in favour of an increase in the allowance to postmasters. I have called the attention of the Postmaster General to the case of a postmaster who has been in the service for 43 years, who keeps a post office in which a daily mail is received, and who only gets $30 a year. No allowance is Mr. LEMIEUX
made for rent for the building. He may make something on the sale of postage stamps, but that cannot amount to very much, and I am glad to hear to-night that the Postmaster General is soon to take this matter into his consideration. I hope my friend the postmaster to whom I have referred will live long enough to be able to participate in the increase which the Postmaster General is going to give these officials. I trust the minister will be able to meet the views of my hon. friend from Elgin and make it $60 if he can. With regard to letter carriers, we have two letter carriers in the city of Halifax who had the misfortune during the early winter to slip and become disabled. I understand that these letter carriers have not been paid during the time they were idle.

My hon. friend might send me'their names? Generally in these cases we pay them their time as if they had been at work provided they accompany their claim with the certificate of a doctor. The treasury board has to pass upon such claims, and the treasury board sits when it can. There is a heap of papers before the treasury board at present, and I think that these two cases are included in the recommendations which I have sent in. At all events, my hon. friend might send me their names.

I will be pleased to do that. It would be nothing but fair that a medical certificate should accompany any claim of the kind. I am glad to hear that the matter is under consideration. With regard to railway mail clerks, we have the statement of the Postmaster General very definitely that the government have come to the conclusion that they could not make the minimum salary more than $500. I regret that that is the case, but I will not take up the time of the committee upon the subject, as a good many arguments have been presented from this side of the House in support of the claim that this amount should be increased. Then, some rule has been made with regard to the age of postal clerks. As a matter of fact, the Postmaster General knows that there are not very many men 18 years of age in the railway mail service. Generally we find them from 20 years up. A very strong argument could be made to show why these men should receive more than $500. Five hundred dollars means $9 a week. Reference has been made to the high cost of living in the west, but the Postmaster General is arranging for reciprocity so that things will he very cheap in the west, and the west will be helped in that regard.
How about reciprocity in the east?

It is not going to touch us very much down there. You are looking for cheap living in the west, and you are likely to get it. While 25 or 30 years ago a young man in Halifax could get a respectable boarding house for $3.50 or $4 a week, to-day a young man cannot get board and lodging in any respectable place in any city at less than $7 a week, therefore, we have a young man starting in the railway mail service with barely enough to pay his board. Some reference was made to young men starting in banks. There is no comparison at all, because a young man goes into a bank to learn the business. He learns how to water stock, and a great many other things, and perhaps in a short time he can go out, organize a merger, make money, and become rich, whereas the poor railway mail clerk will never make a merger unless he runs one car into another, loses his ' life, and leaves a widow and children unprovided for, because he cannot save much out of 'his $9 a week. That is the condition that the railway mail clerk faces every day, whereas the other man is exposed to no danger whatever. He has cuffs and collars, and a nice tie, and he meets nice people, and if he happens to be in the ladies branch where nobody but ladies are permitted to go he has pleasure all the day long. The banks, particularly in western Canada cannot get clerks, and they are bringing young; men out from the old country and paying their passage. The other day I had the great pleasure of travelling with fifty young Irishmen who Were coming out to - the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
Nothing too good for the Irish.
If there is anything good they are going to look after it. I was talking to these young men
Will they learn to water stock?

If they get acquainted with my hon. friend he will be able to teach them something about that or about any other kind of stock. These young men had all their expenses paid, and they were starting at not less than $600 a year, and were learning a business besides. I am not an expert in physiognomy as I ought to be, I have learned most of what I know about it from looking at the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I should say that these young men were from eighteen years to twenty-one years, and they were starting out in a far better position than young Canadians could start in the post office service of the country. The banks are taking our money from the east to the west and they are sending our young men after it, but they don't stay in the banks out
west, they go on farms and get rich and the first thing you know they are able to spend the winter in England. The reason you get good men in the east to fill these poisitions is that our farms are not very enticing, our manufacturing industries are not as great as we hope they will be, and our railway facilities are inadequate, especially in the maritime provinces, and there is lacking diversity of employment to keep our young men at home. We all know that the minimum of $500 is too small and that is admitted by the Postmaster General himself. But, now that he is proposing this resolution, he should urge on his colleagues to make the increase $100 a year until the maximum is reached. It does seem to me that with the knocking about a railway mail clerk gets on a train he has to be of pretty good stuff to live the fifteen years which entitles him to get the maximum under the proposal of the Postmaster General. When the Postmaster General spoke of a man getting promotion in the post office service if he had ' grit ' enough in him, I take it that he did not mean grit in the sense we generally understand it, and I say this in case some of my friends over here who are less scrupulous than I ,am may use that expression against the Postmaster General when the elections come around. In view of the surplus of $750,000 in the Post Office Department, the Postmaster General should not be niggardly with his employees, and I am confident that if he uses his persuasive powers on his colleagues he can get them to assent to our proposition that the increase should be $100 per annum and should not be limited to $50 after the first three years. I trust that the Postmaster General will make provision in the Bill that the railway mail clerks, instead of having an increase of $100 a year for the first three years only, will have an increase of $100 a year until they reach the maximum of $1,400.

I want to congratulate the Postmaster General on increasing the salaries of the smaller officers. I had the pleasure of attending the meeting held by the postmasters. of the Dominion, and at that time, if I remember rightly, I drew the attention of the Postmaster General to the special conditions that exist in western Canada. Take my own county, for instance. It is a very large county, and we have not the advantages of good roads. It is a prairie country, and in rainy seasons the roads are very muddy, and the people who come for their mail leave the post office in a condition that it is worth almost all that the postmaster gets for the week to clean it out. I would like to impress on the Postmaster General that there is a great difference between the districts in Canada regarding the remuneration

which a postmaster ought to get. In many cases it is a great sacrifice on the part of these people to keep the post office. The remuneration of the country postmasters in the country west of the lakes really ought to be more than $50 a year, though I appreciate the action of the Postmaster General in increasing it to that amount.

Not to $50, but to $35.
Mr. BRADBURY Well, I am disappointed, because I understood that this Bill was to increase it to $50. I felt satisfied that those representing the postmasters of the Dominion had made a good case.
I stated a moment ago that I was considering the question. It would not come under this Bill, because the postmasters do not come under the Civil Service Act.

Perhaps it will suit my purpose to leave the question open, as it will give the Postmaster General an opportunity to deal with that phase of it which I am bringing to his attention. In addition to what I have said, a postmaster who keeps an office in an isolated situation in the province of Manitoba often has to entertain his neighbours who come to get their mail about meal time.

I may say to my hon. friend that since I had that interview with the Association of Postmasters, and the members of the House, I have started to prepare a scale which the House may know of before the session is over.

The postmasters also brought before the Postmaster General the question of supplies for the country post offices. That is a very small request. There are more supplies wasted here during the session than would perhaps supply half the post offices in Canada. I think the minister should provide supplies of that kind to the post offices, especially those that deal with registered letters, and things of that kind.

I regret that I cannot see my way clear to add to the floral tributes which haye been handed to the Postmaster General to-night, because I do not think the Post Office Department has any right to have a surplus of three-quarters of a million. I do not think there is any credit due to the head of that department for having such a surplus. Every cent of it comes directly out of the people, and should go back to the people in more efficient mail service. Therefore, I do not feel like throwing bouquets so long as there are people in my constituency, as the Postmaster General knows very well there are, who have to travel 5, 6, 7 or 8 miles for their mail. When the Postmaster General Mr. BRADBURY
raises the salaries of the country postmasters I will throw .my bouquets, but it is a little soon to do it now. The country people of Ontario are not getting a fair share of the post office revenue, and so long as that state of things exists, and people have to go down on their knees and beg facilities which should he granted to them, without a moment's hesitation, and when there is a large surplus in the treasury, every member who represents a rural constituency should rise and make his protest.

I agree with my hon. friend from Frontenac that while we have a surplus of three-quarters of a million dollars many of the rural parts of Ontario are getting very poor service. In my riding there are places where there is a mail only every other day, and other places where there is a mail only twice a week. I made application for a daily mail, and I had good reason to believe that the hon. Postmaster General, was going to grant it, but apparently there was not revenue enough to pay for the service, and we did not get 'it. If we are establishing rural mail delivery in many places, there are. many others which are badly neglected; and if we have the money, there is no reason why 'we should not give the people better mail service. Another subject which my hon. friend from Elgin (Air. Crothers) spoke of was the poorly paid postmasters in the rural .parts of Ontario. $50 is absolutely nothing. In many offices, it will not pay to sweep them out. The minister says that while $35 is the minimum, the postmaster has a commission on the stamps he sells. But many of these offices where 'they serve many people with their mails, have a very small sale of stamps. In my county there are a couple of offices which are four miles from the village and which, while they handle the mails of four or five father offices for the accommodation of the people, have a very small sale of Stamps because the people buy them in the village. I think $60 surely should be the .minimum paid for any post office in the country. There is no reason why we should ask any one to keep a room for the postal accommodation of the people for less than that.

I am sure the Postmaster General can see that the best way out of the difficulty with the country postmasters is to increase rural free mail delivery. I am sure he will take into consideration the increase from $800 up to $1,400 at possibly $100 per year until the limit is reached if the Civil Service Act will allow it. Would he say when we are likely to have the railway mail clerks and those in the city post offices come under the Civil Service Act? Judging from the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton (Air. Carvell) and the

minister himself, I would conclude that there are plenty of applicants; and if these applicants come under the Civil Service Commission, I am satisfied that the Postmaster General will be rid of a great deal of trouble anl have no difficulty in obtaining employees.

I could not tell exactly when the outside service in the larger post offices, such as Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec and Winnipeg will come under the Civil Service Act. In my judgment we should bring them under it as early as possible, and that is the view shared 'by other members of the government and of the House. But there are difficulties in the way which will have to be overcome. I hope that within a year or so I shall be able to nut these large offices under the operation of the Civil Service Act.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Frontenac, that when we have such a large surplus we should change in many places our mail delivery, and have the mails delivered twice a week or three times a week instead of once. There is nothing to boast of in a large surplus when we have such inefficient service, especially in the rural districts. Really $35 a year is scarcely sufficient to pay for cleaning out the post office room. The amount should be at least $100 or $2 a week. I have an application from the county of Carleton for a small section of rural mail delivery Which I trust the minister will take into consideration and deal with favourably.

I simply rise to say that I heartily endorse an increase for the small offices. I quite understand that the Postmaster General has in his mind to do something for these offices and purposes at an early date bringing the minimum up to $50. This country is big enough and rich enough to pay that. There is no reason why people living in the country should keep their houses open for the accommodation of their neighbours for the small sum of $50 and, perhaps, the minister's generosity will add something to that. I leave it in his hands and have no doubt he will be as fair as he can. With regard to railway mail clerks, they are, perhaps, entitled to more consideration than any other class in the service, owing to the more hazardous nature of their employment. I believe the Postmaster General has that idea fairly in his mind and is keeping that in view in arranging their salaries. With regard to the letter carriers, they are a class whom we do not have in my county, beyond a few rural mail deliveries which I believe are working very successfully. I am sorry that that system has not been further extended, but still I have no hesitation in expressing my opinion that the mail carriers are fairly
well paid. We hear a great' deal about the increased cost of living, particularly in the west, but it would be more accurate to speak of the increased extravagance of the people, and if we did that we would not have so many applications for increases in salary. The increased cost of living was one of those things that came about the time the Liberals came into power and a great deal is made of it. I trust that the Postmaster General will do justice, particularly to the smaller post offices; but there is a middle class of post offices in towns with a population of 1,200 or 2,000. In these the public are much more exacting than they were 20 or 25 years ago. For instance, if a postmaster were now to lock up the post office and go to dinner, as they used to do, the Postmaster General 'would probably receive a wire complaining of that, so that the postmaster is obliged to employ more help and more efficient help and he needs more revenue to do that. I hope the Postmaster General will do his best to assist this class of postmasters.
Mr. LEA1IEUX. Hear, hear.

The rural mail delivery system can be operated most properly and successfully in Prince Edward Island because that province is much more thickly settled in proportion to its area than any other in Canada, and I hope if this system is generally inaugurated we will have our full share of it. I also think the salaries to the rural postmasters are too small, the minimum should be increased from $35 to $50.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
